newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi denies bombing, may face Canada deportation.
newsitem.headline: Saudi denies bombing, may face Canada deportation.

text.p: A Saudi Shi'ite Muslim in a Canadian prison who faces possible deportation over his alleged involvement in a Saudi bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen denied on Monday being in the kingdom at the time.

"I was astonished to be accused, and especially to be accused of being the driver of the (get-away) car," Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh told reporters from behind a glass partition in the maximum security visiting area.

A U.S. law enforcement official in Washington said that based on interviews conducted by Saudi Arabia of other alleged participants in the attack, Sayegh was suspected of being the driver of a get-away car used after the bombing.
"We think he's an inner-circle person, a support person. He wasn't a bit player," the official said. "He's a good suspect."

A U.S. sergeant on guard at the time of the June 25 blast, which also injured 500 people, reported a fuel truck driving up to a U.S. military-housing complex in eastern Saudi Arabia. The passengers in the truck piled into an accompanying car and drove off, he reported. Four minutes later the bomb went off.

Sayegh, 28, said he had been in self-imposed exile in Syria from about two years ago until he flew to Ottawa in August -- two months after the bombing -- to apply for refugee status. He said his passport stamps showed this.
Sayegh was polite and soft-spoken. He wore silver-rimmed glasses and a dark blue prison uniform. His hair was neatly groomed and he had a beard that looked several days old.
He was arrested last Tuesday at an Ottawa convenience store and has been in high-security isolation since.

It became clear during the interview that he was a devout Shi'ite Muslim who undertook religious studies in Qom, the main Shi'ite learning center in Iran where the late revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini also studied.
He said he feared going back to Saudi Arabia because of the way the Sunni Muslim rulers treated Shi'ites and said he would not cooperate with any U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation agents.
Sayegh denied any connection to dissident or guerrilla organizations: "I have no relations with any organization. I have relations with the general public."

A Canadian Federal Court judge must review his case by Thursday or Friday. The judge will determine whether there had been grounds to issue the security certificate -- signed by Immigration Minister Lucienne Robillard and Solicitor-General Herb Gray -- that led to his arrest.
If the process was determined to be valid, Sayegh would then appear at an immigration hearing to determine whether he should be deported, Robillard spokesman Benoit Chiquette said.
Robillard on Friday indicated a willingness to deport -- or "remove" -- people who are security risks even if there was a possibility that they could face the death penalty abroad.

The FBI said on Saturday it hoped to be able to question Sayegh about the bombing, but Gray spokesman Dan Brien said he was unaware of any request so far from Washington or Riyadh for his extradition.
Sayegh is being detained at an Ottawa prison where another Saudi, Fahad al-Shehri, is also held.

Canadian officials say Shehri was arrested in December after he sought refugee status, supposedly because he said the Saudi government wanted him in connection with the bombing. He denies involvement in the bombing, however, and both Saudi and U.S. officials deny any interest in him.
